nameStory: The 'garlic' in garlic penny-cress comes from the distinctive garlicky smell you'll notice when you crush the leaves or stems. The 'penny-cress' part refers to the small, round, flattened seed pods that reminded early botanists of tiny coins or pennies hanging from the stems.
description: Garlic penny-cress is a slender, upright annual plant that typically grows 10 to 26 inches tall. It's a member of the mustard family, featuring small white flowers arranged in clusters at the top of the stem. The plant has a somewhat weedy appearance and thrives in disturbed areas like roadsides and field edges. Originally from Europe, it has made itself at home in parts of New England as an introduced species.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Crush a leaf or stem between your fingers and you'll immediately smell a strong garlic or onion-like odor - this is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in small, dense clusters at the stem tips, typical of the mustard family

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round, flattened seed pods that look like tiny pennies dangling from short stalks along the upper stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are somewhat spoon-shaped, while upper stem leaves are narrow and clasp around the stem with small ear-like projections

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Erect, unbranched or sparingly branched annual that stands upright like a small green sentinel along disturbed ground

habitat: Look for garlic penny-cress along roadsides, in disturbed fields, construction sites, and other areas where the soil has been disrupted. It thrives in sunny spots with poor to moderately fertile soil and seems to particularly enjoy the edge zones where human activity meets wild spaces.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin growing rapidly, with the characteristic garlic scent already detectable in the leaves.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full height and produce their clusters of small white flowers, followed by the development of the distinctive penny-like seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Mature seed pods turn brown and split open to release seeds, while the entire plant begins to die back as an annual.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, but seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Despite being called 'garlic' penny-cress, this plant is completely unrelated to actual garlic - the similar smell comes from sulfur compounds that the plant produces as a defense mechanism against hungry insects and herbivores.
confusionNotes: It can be confused with other small white-flowered mustards, but the garlic smell when crushed is unmistakable. The round, flattened seed pods also distinguish it from most other mustard family plants, which typically have longer, narrow pods.
contextualKnowledge: This European native has been in North America for over a century but remains relatively uncommon compared to other introduced mustards. Its scientific name recently changed from Thlaspi alliaceum to Mummenhoffia alliacea as botanists better understood its relationships.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England, garlic penny-cress is most similar to other penny-cresses in the genus Thlaspi. However, it's distinguished by its strong garlic odor and preference for disturbed habitats, while most Thlaspi species are scentless mountain plants. The round seed pods also help separate it from the more common mustard weeds with elongated pods.
